_comment: The attack surface each project is ALLOWED to have. scripts/surface.mjs
compares this against what the manifests and the source actually do, and
fails when a project exceeds its budget.
This file is the security card in every project's README, in machine-
readable form. The README says '01 asks for no permissions'; this is what
stops that sentence from quietly becoming false. Growing a budget is a
deliberate edit to a reviewed file, which is the point: the diff that adds
a permission is the diff a reviewer needs to see.
Every complete project must appear here. An unlisted project fails rather
than being skipped — otherwise adding 04-something would escape the
budget entirely by having no budget.

why: Two hosts, repository-wide: Temporal Cloud, and a local `temporal server start-dev`.
A content script matching anything else — and above all <all_urls> or *://*/* —
means the extension runs on pages that have nothing to do with Temporal.
Self-hosted UIs live on hosts we cannot enumerate, so a fork adds its own host
here on purpose; that is a decision, not a default.
Every one of these turns workflow data into executable markup or code.
The extension renders strings it did not author — workflow ids, types, task
queue names — into a page it does not own. `textContent` cannot execute;
`innerHTML` can, and a workflow id is a perfectly good place to hide a
payload. There is no allowance list here on purpose: if a project ever needs
one of these, that is an edit to this file plus a written reason, reviewed.
WHICH packages a project may have is deliberately not budgeted here, and this
note is what stops that reading as an oversight. The policy is still the same:
browser APIs and code in this repository for anything specific to this
extension — the page-world technique, the request ledger, what may be sent to a
codec server, what is rendered as text — and mature, maintained libraries for
generic algorithms. Each project's README carries the table, with a reason per
package; `npm run measure` prints what is really in the bundles.
What was removed is the machinery: per-project direct/also_bundled lists
checked against esbuild's metafile, plus a rule that every bundled package be
documented in the README at its installed version and licence. It worked, and
it cost more to read than it caught.
ONE rule was kept, as surface.mjs rule 9: every third-party package that enters
a bundle through a project's own source must be declared in THAT project's
dependencies — esbuild's metafile answers it, so it covers what reaches a
browser and not an import erased before bundling. It is the one a
reviewer cannot get from a lockfile diff — the projects share a single hoisted
install, so a package a SIBLING declares resolves from this one, and adding an
import of it changes neither package.json nor the lockfile while esbuild inlines
it into a content script.
What that gives up, stated plainly: nothing mechanical announces a new
TRANSITIVE package, and nothing checks the version or licence of any of them. A
dependency diff grants the extension no new capability — it is not a manifest
permission diff — but it is an audit-surface diff, and for a transitive package
a reviewer has to read the lockfile to see it.
No gate can read a binary. Not this one, not the leak gate, not any secret
scanner — so a committed image is a file nobody reviews. The icons are
exempt because they are GENERATED from arithmetic by scripts/make-icons.mjs;
the reviewable artefact is that script.
Adding a screenshot or a GIF means adding it here, and it must have been
captured against `temporal server start-dev` with synthetic workflow names.
A recording of a real tenant cannot be redacted after the fact.

01-family-tree.why: The whole claim of this project is that a useful view costs nothing. No permissions key, no service worker, and no chrome.* call in src/ — enforced here and by tsconfig.json's "types": [].

02-techniques.why: One permission, `storage`, for the user's own deep-link templates and toggles. Still no host_permissions — but read the next sentences, because this project DOES originate requests and no manifest key says so. Two per running row: one history-reverse page of one event for the `Last event` column, and one DescribeWorkflowExecution for the retrying-activity badge (pendingActivities is in no other response, which is the justification for the whole request path). Both are issued from the page's own world, by src/page/pageApi.ts and nothing else, where a host permission would buy nothing: Chrome treats a content-script fetch as cross-origin even with one. There is ONE gate, not one per feature — fetchForListedRun() is the only route to the page's Authorization header and it checks the ledger itself, so a feature added later cannot forget to. Those two are the only requests this project ORIGINATES and both go to the host the page is already on; no setting can add another, it decodes no payload, and the retry badge deliberately does not read lastFailure.message, so nothing here reads application data. Identifiers do leave this page, by exactly one route: a deep-link template names a host the user chose, and clicking the link navigates the browser there with the ids visible in the URL — a navigation the user starts, with no body and no credential of ours. The deep-link card on a single workflow's page fetches nothing at all — it reads responses the page fetched for itself, through the watcher seam in pageApi.ts, which touches neither the ledger nor the credentials. The codec server — the first host this extension POSTs a body to, without any navigation — and the personal-data question arrive together in stage 03, the payload stage. A permission diff is not a capability diff; the audit for this project is that security card, not this list alone.

03-payloads.why: THE SAME MANIFEST BUDGET AS 02, AND THAT IS THE WARNING THIS ENTRY EXISTS TO CARRY. One permission, `storage`, no host_permissions, no service worker, the same three content-script matches — every capability-bearing key is identical, and a manifest diff against 02 shows the name, the description, the version and the button's tooltip. It bundles the same two packages as 02, too: this stage adds none of its own, having tried three ways to format JSON and kept none of them. What changed is the capability: 02 can put identifiers into a link you click, whereas this project POSTs payload bytes to a host you named, on hover, with no navigation and nothing to look at first — it is also the first that decodes payloads at all, and therefore the first whose panel can hold personal or financial data. No manifest key says any of that, and no permission budget can, which is why this entry is the floor and not the audit. The audit is the security card in 03-payloads/README.md, where the egress is described request-for-request, the two credential options are shown as deliberate deletions, and the residual forged-message risk is stated once at full width along with the argument for accepting it. The egress claims are asserted from outside the extension in 03-payloads/tests/unit/apiInjectCodec.spec.ts, and the endpoint policy they rest on in 03-payloads/tests/unit/codec.spec.ts.

04-ui-goodies.why: THE SAME MANIFEST BUDGET AS 03, ONCE AGAIN ON PURPOSE. One permission, `storage`, no host_permissions, no service worker, the same three content-script matches — a manifest diff against 03 shows only the name, the description, the version and the button's tooltip. Every capability this stage adds is presentational, not a new request or a new destination: a lossless JSON viewer over payload text the extension could already read; column reordering, a copy button and a page-size choice that only ever change how already-fetched rows are displayed; a NOT filter and Ctrl/Cmd-click additive filtering that build a query string for Temporal's own list endpoint, the one 02 already calls; and family focus / expand-to-families, which re-run that same query with an added RootWorkflowId or WorkflowId clause rather than opening a second endpoint. Nothing here decodes a payload that was not already decodable, nothing sends a payload anywhere it did not already go, and nothing introduces a second host. The capability worth naming is a new bundled dependency for the JSON viewer's lexer, which does not touch the network at all — rule 9 below covers it being declared in package.json today. The package, its version and the reason it is a lexer rather than a parser, and the full security card comparing this stage's presentational capabilities line by line against 03's, are 04-ui-goodies/README.md content still to be written, deferred to the phase that finishes this stage's docs — see the progress note in that README's Status section in the meantime.
